title: Prostate Cancer Cases Rise 3% Annually as Updated Guidelines Push Earlier Screening
excerpt: The American Cancer Society estimates 333,830 new U.S. diagnoses in 2026, while updated AUA/SUO guidelines lower the recommended screening age and introduce flexible intervals.
body:
• New prostate cancer diagnoses in the U.S. have risen 3% per year since 2014, with an estimated 333,830 cases and 36,320 deaths expected in 2026.
  • Updated AUA/SUO 2026 guidelines lower the recommended screening start to ages 45–50 for average-risk men and 40–45 for high-risk groups, with intervals of every 2–4 years instead of annually.
  • The digital rectal exam is no longer required as a first screening step; PSA blood tests alone are now the preferred starting point.
  • Black men are nearly 70% more likely to be diagnosed and twice as likely to die from prostate cancer compared to White men, making early conversations with a doctor critical.

Rising Diagnoses, Rising Stakes

September marks Prostate Cancer Awareness Month, and the numbers released by the American Cancer Society deliver a mixed message. New prostate cancer cases have climbed 3% annually from 2014 to 2022, with the steepest increase occurring among advanced-stage diagnoses. The ACS Cancer Statistics 2026 report estimates 333,830 new U.S. cases this year and 36,320 deaths.

The increase is partly driven by more men getting screened — which creates opportunities for early intervention — but too many are still being screened too late, according to Dr. William Dahut, chief scientific officer at the American Cancer Society.

"We're seeing two things happen at once: more men are being diagnosed with prostate cancer, and a growing share of those cases are happening at a more advanced stage. That tells us screening conversations are happening too late for too many men."

— Dr. William Dahut, Chief Scientific Officer, American Cancer Society

What the Updated Guidelines Change

The 2026 update to the American Urological Association and Society of Urologic Oncology (AUA/SUO) guideline represents the most significant overhaul of prostate cancer screening recommendations in years. The previous guideline had five core statements; the updated version expands to thirty-five, incorporating MRI imaging, biomarkers, and more individualized risk-based approaches.

The key changes for everyday clinical practice are straightforward. Average-risk men should begin screening conversations between ages 45 and 50 — down from the previous guidance of age 50. High-risk individuals, including men of African ancestry, those carrying BRCA gene mutations, or those with a strong family history, should start as early as age 40 to 45.

Screening intervals have shifted from annual to every 2 to 4 years for most patients, adjusted based on PSA levels, overall health, and life expectancy. The digital rectal exam (DRE), long a standard part of prostate screening, is no longer a required first step. PSA blood testing alone is now the preferred starting point.

"It's not age, it's life expectancy," said Dr. Daniel W. Lin, chair of the AUA guideline update and a urological oncologist. "I see a lot of 70 to 75-year-olds who are going to live 20 years. I see some 60-year-olds who won't live 10 years because of their health."

MRI and Biomarkers Enter the Mainstream

The updated framework gives multiparametric MRI a more prominent role, particularly before repeat biopsies, to improve detection of clinically significant disease while helping avoid unnecessary procedures. Biomarker assays — both blood- and urine-based — can now be used selectively when PSA results are inconclusive.

These tools represent a shift toward combining PSA, imaging, biomarkers, and risk calculators rather than relying on a single threshold to drive decisions. AI-assisted computer-aided diagnostics may further level the playing field by reducing variability between radiologists reading the same MRI, according to Dr. Lin.

Racial Disparities Remain Stark

The data underscores persistent inequities. Black men are nearly 70% more likely to be diagnosed with prostate cancer and twice as likely to die from the disease compared to White men, according to the ACS. When the disease develops in Black men, they tend to be younger.

The AUA guidelines directly address this by recommending earlier screening for men of African ancestry and those carrying BRCA mutations, with some protocols suggesting a PSA threshold as low as 2.5 at age 50 for high-risk groups — a level previously considered normal.

What Men Should Do Now

About one in eight men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer in their lifetime, but the ACS notes that more than 3.5 million men living in the U.S. have survived the disease. Early detection remains the strongest lever for improving outcomes.

The ACS recommends that men at average risk discuss screening with their doctor by age 50. Men at high risk — including those with a family history or of African descent — should have this conversation at 45, and those at the highest risk by age 40. The organization offers a free online risk-assessment tool, ACS CancerRisk360, to help evaluate personal risk factors.
